title: Bank of America hit with $1.2bn fine for money laundering failings
content: Bank of America has been fined $1.2bn (£910m) for failing to detect potential money laundering and other illegal activity, the US Treasury Department said on Tuesday. The banking giant failed to report over $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, $1bn of which posed national security and illicit finance risks, the Treasury said. Those failures included not flagging transactions that possibly involved Chinese money laundering networks or trade-based laundering "with a substantial nexus to the southwest border", according to the Treasury. "Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators," Bank of America told the BBC. The announcement came less 24 hours before Bank of America was due to announce its quarterly earnings on Wednesday morning. "Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share," the bank said in an emailed statement. "We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base," it added. In announcing the fine, the third-largest the department has ever imposed, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks." The Treasury said the bank overly relied on inquiries from outside parties like law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls. This meant that it "effectively outsourced to third parties a substantial portion of its proactive detection and reporting obligations," the department said. As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it "willfully violated" the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money laundering programme, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, the Treasury said. The $1.2bn fine included penalties imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The OCC's $750m fine marked the biggest penalty it has ever levied. OFAC said its settlement with the bank was tied to 475 apparent violations of sanctions programmes including those on Russia and Iran, narcotics, and global terrorism. The settlement amount of $11.6m reflected the determination that Bank of America's apparent violations were "non-egregious", OFAC said. Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died on Monday after police say he was ejected from a ride at a Six Flags amusement park in Georgia. One person has died and others were injured after an incident at a US amusement park. The Legally Blonde actress faces two counts of assault for allegedly kicking a police officer and a nurse after allegedly attacking attendants on a flight. Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room. Davis was found guilty last month over his role in the late rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in 1996. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF
content: Countries around the world have had their future economic prospects assessed by influential body, the International Monetary Fund (IMF). What the IMF says matters – it aims to keep the global economy stable and its twice-yearly forecasts are one of the most authoritative looks at what is really going on around the world. Yet like all forecasts they can also turn out to be incorrect, so they shouldn't be treated as gospel. Here are three things we've learnt about the UK from the IMF's latest report. The global economy has been rocked by the US-Israel war with Iran. The transportation and production of energy in the Middle East has been severely disrupted, causing oil prices to jump and inflation to rise. To calm the rate of price rises, central banks, including the Bank of England, are expected to hike interest rates in the coming months. Despite all this, the IMF said the global economy is doing much better than expected, partly because of the surge of investment into artificial intelligence (AI). And this is good news for the UK. The IMF said its economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027. A growing economy means companies are investing more and hiring more people while shoppers have more money to spend. A shrinking economy means the reverse is true. There is increased concern about how much money countries are borrowing, but the IMF said the UK is doing better than all other major economies at this. The IMF said the UK "basically stands out, along with India" when it comes to addressing the problem and by 2031 it is projected to have the lowest annual borrowing of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US. Sir Howard Davies, former deputy governor of the Bank of England, said this was largely because the UK has a government with a majority which has committed to tackling the situation, which it is expected to achieve either through tax rises, cuts to public services, or a mix of both. By contrast, he says the US has said little about reducing its deficit, while France and Germany don't have majority governments. "So, we [the UK] are not great students, but we look somewhat better than some of the others we are sharing the class with," he said. Meanwhile, the IMF's growth forecasts for the UK mean it is expected to have the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 this year along with Germany. Sir Howard believes this should also be seen in context. "We're still growing slowly. It's almost like saying we're winning a slow bicycle race here because other people are going backwards a bit more rapidly than we are." While the IMF boosted its projection for the UK's growth in 2026, it slightly downgraded its forecasts for next year. While the UK has handled the economic fallout from the Iran war better than expected so far, it says this will change next year as high energy prices and elevated interest rates affect how much people spend in shops and how much companies are willing to invest. In addition, the IMF has said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices. It forecasts inflation in the UK will average 3.3% this year and it has raised its estimate for next year to 2.8% from its previous prediction of 2.4%. "There will be increasing inflationary pressure put on the UK and the Bank of England will have to consider further rate rises," says Tim Armitage, investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot. He added that at least one rate rise is predicted this year, with more expected to come next year. Millions could be entitled to compensation as a result of commission arrangements between lenders and dealers. The leadership team is attempting a buyout, but a union has warned the retailer could fall into administration instead. TFG London has apologised to customers for disruption after it identified a "cybersecurity incident" on Sunday. Heating oil customers facing soaring bills are promised better regulation of the sector by the government. title: Royal Mail losing 400 postal workers a week, says union
content: About 400 postmen and women are leaving Royal Mail per week, according to the Communication Workers Union (CWU), who claims this number has gone up since the company introduced a new delivery system earlier this year. The CWU says the firm had been losing about 330 postal staff a week from a workforce of 83,000 before it rolled out DM26, which reorganised routes to improve delivery performance. The union claims the new system is not working in hundreds of offices, and BBC Your Voice has heard from staff warning of a "nightmare" Christmas ahead as the number of parcels increases. Royal Mail says the reforms are part of its plan to deliver a more "efficient and financially sustainable" service. Over the last year we've been in touch with more than 30 postal staff in all four nations of the UK, as they have switched over to DM26. It allows for second class post to only be delivered every other weekday, and is supposed to guarantee first class mail and parcels are delivered every day, by putting workers into groups of three and changing the walking pattern of rounds. But posties speaking to us anonymously say parcels are still being prioritised, letters left behind, and time wasted in sorting and dividing mail into first and second class. "I didn't take any first class mail out on my last shift because I was on a road that's been behind for weeks," a worker in the West Midlands told me. "But I'm sure a manager would have ticked a box to say all first class mail went out." A Royal Mail spokesperson said the company always worked to ensure all mail - both letters and parcels - were delivered on time. Some postal workers we've spoken to say the new model is also increasing their workload. We asked eight workers in different areas to track their average step counts. Since the switchover all their steps increased by a quarter or even a third, often up to around 25,000 steps a day. Several fear this Christmas will be a "nightmare". "We all think this Christmas will be the worst ever, for us and our customers," said one postman in the East Midlands. Bryn Dymott delivered post in the village of Wootton in Bedfordshire for nine years. For the most part he loved the job. But he left the company in July saying he couldn't face another "shambolic" Christmas. "People put things in the post for them to be delivered, not for them to be delayed because Royal Mail hasn't got the systems in place and enough people to get them delivered." Bryn says he wanted to speak out after leaving the company because he was sick of the fact that posties aren't able to say what's really happening. He says the company is "proving it's impossible to have four people's work done by three people. It shouldn't really come as a surprise." So far DM26 has been introduced in about 1,000 of Royal Mail's 1,200 delivery offices. Now the CWU has told its members to pause further roll-out of the new system until a plan can be agreed with Royal Mail to address problems. The union says that while it is operating successfully in around 500 offices, it has run into significant problems in hundreds of others. "Put simply, if a boat is already taking on water, adding more passengers is unlikely to solve the problem," says Martin Walsh of the CWU. The union said most Royal Mail workers leaving the company were believed to be new starters on part-time contracts, but also said there had been an increase in staff on legacy contracts departing. Royal Mail, on the other hand, says the new system is on track to be up and running in all offices by Christmas. It says the roll-out is 90% complete and that it is now delivering to "95% of addresses every day across the UK, up from 88% before the roll-out. The roll-out continues across our network and we expect quality of service to improve as deployment progresses." The company says it is hiring, as usual, an additional 22,000 temporary workers over the Christmas period. Royal Mail has battled with increased competition and falling demand for letter deliveries in recent years, and last week announced plans to cut 2,500 head office and other supporting roles by the end of 2027. The company has also faced years of criticism from politicians and the public over slow letter deliveries - something which has continued since the new system has been rolled out. The regulator Ofcom has fined Royal Mail more than £37m in the last three years for missing delivery targets. But some MPs think it is time for a new approach, and a group of them will meet the regulator later on Wednesday. "We need to think outside the box," Dave Robertson, Labour MP for Lichfield, Burntwood and the Villages in Staffordshire. "We need to bring as many people to the table on this to make sure we come up with a long-term solution because what's been tried up to now clearly isn't working." An Ofcom spokesperson said not only has it issued fines to Royal Mail in recent years but it has also demanded an improvement plan and reformed the obligations imposed on the company, adding: "We will continue to hold it to account using the full extent of the powers available to us." Postal Services Minister Kate Dearden said Royal Mail's improvement plan was "a step in the right direction, but it must deliver tangible improvements for customers. We will continue to hold them to account on their performance." Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. title: Not building third runway would be 'huge missed opportunity', warns Heathrow boss
content: Not building a third runway at Heathrow Airport would be a "huge missed opportunity" for the UK, the boss of the country's busiest airport has warned. Thomas Woldbye told BBC Radio 4's Today programme it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say whether he backed expansion. The airport's chief executive said if its owners could not invest in a third runway, the money "will be invested somewhere else in the world", suggesting a decision would be made in the new year. The Department for Transport said it was reviewing responses to a consultation and was "considering the appropriate next steps". A spokesperson added that the government supported airport expansion "across the country where this can contribute to growth and opportunity, while meeting the tests on the environment". They said expanding Heathrow had the "potential to deliver around £40 billion in economic benefits across the country". Building a third runway at Heathrow has been debated for decades. The project has proved controversial, facing steep opposition from local residents, politicians and climate campaigners. Last year, then-chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying that "a third runway is badly needed", and that the government could not "duck the decision any longer". Heathrow Airport is owned by a consortium of investors, the largest of which is French private equity firm Ardian. Others include the Qatar Investment Authority, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and the China Investment Corporation. "If they cannot invest in Heathrow... then that money will be invested somewhere else in the world," Woldbye said. "It's not about allocating this money elsewhere. It's private money. It's not public money. So hence, it will not go into the UK. I think that would be really a sad, huge missed opportunity for this country." A third runway would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway. It is estimated it would cost £33bn to build. Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built. This additional traffic would potentially lead to a huge surge in revenue for the airport's owners, and Heathrow has argued the expansion would provide a "huge economic boost" and create jobs. The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues. Whether the new-look government still backs a third runway is not yet clear. Burnham, who as Mayor of Greater Manchester opposed the scheme, said he believed the matter was "for London and Londoners". "I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he said, speaking to the BBC last month . Woldbye said he hoped the prime minister would "will come along" with the project, pointing out it was backed by the unions. He added that a third runway was "not just for Londoners". "Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK." Downing Street declined to comment on Woldbye's remarks. Questioned about the noise impact on nearby communities of more planes taking off and landing, Woldbye claimed Heathrow had seen a "stark" reduction in noise over the past 40 years and said the "trend will continue". "My biggest concern is actually the years of uncertainty. And I think it's time that we give them certainty on what we want with this project so that we can move on and they can move on in their lives," he said. Woldbye told the Today programme he had not yet met the current Chancellor John Healey, but if he did, he would outline that the airport "contributes dramatically to the economy" but that "we are now full". "That means we will stop contributing or stop growing that contribution. If we want to avoid that, we need to now take this decision, move forward and continue the work of the previous government to move at speed and deliver this," he said. The Department for Transport said it was still finalising its Airports National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow. It was last updated in 2018. Woldbye said Heathrow was working on a planning application which has planned to submit in the next couple of years, but said any decision would be guided by government's the national policy statement. The prime minister is calling for partners to step up support for Ukraine following Trump's criticism of Zelensky. Andy Burnham says his government would explore restoring services to the Kent hub. title: Poundland in rescue talks as owners seek buyer
content: Retail chain Poundland is in talks with potential buyers as it seeks a rescue deal, it has confirmed. Executives are working with an Irish property development group on a management buyout, as first reported by Sky News . But a union representing shopworkers warned that the retailer could fall into administration if that deal falls through, putting thousands of jobs at risk. This outcome would be "a disaster for our members", the Usdaw union said. Poundland has about 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, and 12,000 employees. The chain has been struggling for a number of years due to pressures including rising costs and competition. However, it expects sales to have grown more than 3% in 2026 compared with the previous year, which managing director Barry Williams said earlier this month was evidence that its recovery plan "is working". The retailer was sold for £1 last summer by previous owner Pepco to US investment firm Gordon Brothers. The current owners are in the process of seeking buyers, with the Poundland management attempting a buyout, a spokesman said. Mr Williams, along with the firm's leadership team and Andy Bond, a former chairman of Pepco, have been working with Irish real estate firm Martin Property Group on a management buyout. Martin Property Group is the management team's "preferred partner", the spokesman said, but the team will "work with whoever can deliver the best result for the business, colleagues and suppliers and build on the successful recovery that's already taking shape," he added. However, Bally Auluk, a national officer at Usdaw, said there are "deep concerns that the business could go into administration" should this buyout fail. "We are aware that a management buy-out has been attempted and we are told that their offers are being turned down," he added. A Poundland source disputed this, however, saying the Martin Property Group is part of the sale process and remains the management team's preferred partner. Retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth said there were "tough times" on the High Street for all retailers. She said retailers were struggling with "significantly subdued consumer confidence as prices continue to rise" due to higher fuel costs. Poundland itself faces intense competition from rivals including B&M, Aldi, Lidl and from online retailers including Temu and TikTok Shop. The business "lost its strong £1 identity leaving shoppers to think it was getting too expensive", Shuttleworth said, and a costly expansion into clothing and frozen food under past management had not been successful. However, increased sales this year showed a deal with Mr Williams as boss "would make good sense", she added. Oldrids & Co Ltd says it is in "advanced discussions" regarding its Boston site. The influential economics body has upgraded its UK growth forecast for this year, but risks remain. TFG London has apologised to customers for disruption after it identified a "cybersecurity incident" on Sunday. The Post Office is urgently looking for a replacement branch after TG Jones is boarded up. John Holmes started his business in the 1960s and had shops in places like Swindon, Bristol and Cheltenham. title: Global financial system is failing developing countries, says Ed Miliband
content: The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband , will claim the global financial system is failing developing countries, as he calls for a “new deal” for governments struggling under the burden of debt. Promising to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind urgent reform, he will evoke the example of the Gleneagles summit under the last Labour government in 2005 – the culmination of the Make Poverty History campaign. “The global financial system and indeed the global order is failing to serve developing countries on debt, on resilience and on climate. This is not just against our values but against our national interest,” Miliband is expected to say. “In the interconnected world we live in, more than ever, the opportunities and challenges we confront are collective.” Speaking in Bangkok on Wednesday, he will call for the World Bank and other multilateral development banks (MDBs) to use the resources they have available to lighten the load for governments trapped by hefty borrowing costs. “We need action on developing country debt through the MDBs,” he is expected to say. “Action that leverages the balance sheets of the international financial institutions to support these countries to repay over longer time horizons, and crucially, refinancing, with better rates, to give them precious fiscal space.” The foreign secretary will be in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings. He opted to take up the UK’s seat on the bank’s board himself instead of leaving it to the development minister, Kirsty McNeill. Labour’s manifesto in 2024 promised to restore the UK’s international reputation on development issues – but Keir Starmer subsequently slashed the aid budget to pay for defence. Campaigners have long claimed the high interest rates paid by many developing countries mean the repayments crowd out vital public spending – including on tackling the climate emergency. In sub-Saharan Africa, more than three times as much is spent on debt servicing as on education. Miliband will argue that making the global financial system work better for emerging economies will also help to attract more private investment – a key aim of the World Bank under the current president, Ajay Banga. The UK is due to take up the presidency of the G20 group of nations next year – a key global forum for discussing global financial issues, including sovereign debt, which includes emerging economies such as China, India, South Africa and Brazil. The chancellor, John Healey , will set out his own G20 priorities in Bangkok later this week, including mobilising more resources from the balance sheets of the IMF and the World Bank. Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion When the UK held the chair of the narrower G8 group in 2005, at the leaders’ summit at the Gleneagles hotel the UK secured agreements that eventually resulted in more than 30 countries receiving large-scale debt write-downs. Miliband will say resources are now more constrained – but as well as debt refinancing for a large number of countries, he will demand an overhaul of the “common framework” for restructuring the debts of countries unable to pay. The framework is widely criticised as too slow and cumbersome. Among other reforms, the UK wants to see changes to ensure private creditors cannot hold up negotiations – as has happened in recent cases including that of Ethiopia. The foreign secretary will also call for overhauls to allow help to be made available more rapidly to countries in trouble. “We need finance teed up in advance of crises, so that governments get support in days, not months,” he will say. Miliband will be speaking at the launch of a report by the Rockefeller Foundation thinktank, which calls for a “surge” in affordable financing from the IMF and the World Bank to debt-burdened countries. Tim Jones, the policy director of the campaign group Debt Justice, welcomed Miliband’s focus on the issue but said a litmus test of any plan would be whether private sector creditors bear some of the costs. “Action on debt relief is urgently needed. That must include private lenders sharing in the cost. Otherwise public money will just bail out private lenders rather than be used for investment.”
